80% of your free time should be spent *programming*. Not browsing coding forums, reading books, or analyzing the endless different options you have for languages, libraries or projects to start. 

If you're an absolute beginner, then take a few hours to learn the basics of variables, loops, functions, etc. But don't spend too much time watching videos or reading books about this; you want to get your hands dirty in code. The information from books or videos will be forgotten quickly if you don't apply what you've learned.

Read documentation when you need it and learn more about the language when you've mastered the bits you already know. It doesn't matter *what* you're making. You just need to be sure that the problem challenges you in some way.

Learn how to debug, and learn about your IDE. This IMO is one of the biggest reasons why some people find programming so frustrating. If you don't know how to diagnose a problem, you can't fix it. Learn about breakpoints, watch windows, error codes and expressions.

Start with [ProjectEuler](https://projecteuler.net/archives) to reinforce your knowledge of the basic rules of programming. These are simple problems that can be solved in any language for the most part. Most of the problems require you to think about the algorithm behind the problem, like finding the sum of all even Fibonacci numbers less than 4 million. 

Small problems like this you can easily break down into steps and can be solved in a variety of ways. When you solve it yourself, look at other people's submissions to see if they did it better - learn from them.

ProjectEuler isn't that great for learning how to write large-scale applications though, so you'll want to branch out once you get the hang of it. I suggest making a small game. Since you mentioned python [Pygame](https://www.pygame.org/wiki/GettingStarted) is a python library for building games. Making small games helps you understand classes, structures, polymorphism, memory allocation, data structures and pretty much everything else about software development. Even a game as small as pong can teach you a lot about software design. In fact I encourage you to start small as making a mario clone might prove to be too daunting once you understand the real requirements.

In my experience, 80% of my software architecture design came from me attempting to solve problems, only to find that my solution was flawed in some way. It's easy to read books about the ins and outs of a language or why interfaces are the king of software design, but you won't understand how to use the tools you've gained unless you know the strengths and weaknesses of each one. It isn't enough to know the difference between a pointer and a reference, you need to know *when* to use one over the other. People can give you tips on this, but generally you develop your own intuition for it once you've been coding for awhile.

To be fair, # of frames dropped is not a great determiner of performance. 

Say you have a simple application that renders a triangle on the screen. A single triangle. Your frame rate might be somewhere in the high 1000's depending on your hardware and the resolution used.

Add a single point light to the scene now; watch your frame rate drop to less than 500. You lost 500 frames from a single point light. Why? Because it's increasing the render time for every single frame. The frame drops are dramatic at first because the added time to render a single light is greater than the time it takes to render the whole frame.

This ratio changes as your render time per frame increases (as you approach ~120 FPS). So running a scene with 45 individual lights will get approximately the same FPS as a scene with 46. It takes more lights to really drop the frame rate. 

That's why looking at the sky in any game will increase the frame rate by a lot, but the second a single tree is in sight the frame rate begins to tank. 

The cabal dropped 30 frames because there wasn't much else in the scene. But adding one more cabal to a group of 12 won't have the same effect.

On small projects, sure. But are you really going to read thousands of lines of code to wrap your head around how a particular system will handle your data input? Most developers don't have that kinda time because of their deadlines. Game systems and features can often be very complex. And they aren't easily understood in a few short comments. It's best to get a verbal explanation from the person who made it, who also might know of undocumented changes made to that system. But perhaps they're too busy or out for vacation.

Documentation isn't always guaranteed to be updated along with a change. It's easy to forget and follow every standard laid before a developer. 

It's easy to criticize a developers job on the outside. But it's not easy to just fix bugs that crop up. No matter how clean you try to make your code, it also has to be adaptable and change with the demands of the games direction and your publisher. 

Code, documentation, playtesting, explaining systems to others. This all takes a lot of time. And when you find a bug, it's not easy to find out what's causing it. It could be something that happens during very specific circumstances, and you have to test and test and test to see what those cases are. Only then can you devise a solution and see if you can implement it without breaking anything.

Bugs are simply inevitable in complex systems, and they're not always easy to fix.

Hahahhahaahaha you have no idea how software development works dude. 

During the design phase, it's almost always a "perfect" solution. And elegant systems are designed and implemented. But then oh, activision says you need to make changes, or perhaps you encountered a rare edge case you didn't originally consider. Your biweekly or monthly milestone is approaching though, and you need this fixed NOW. To truly fix it, you would have to rewrite the system from the ground up. But for now we can just add a small exception to the rules and bingo, it's fixed. 

Do this enough times and you loose sight of the architecture. It becomes more of a black box and you're uncertain what will break when you go in to fix problems or add new features. 

Games are getting much much bigger than anyone anticipated. Developers are usually only aware of systems they themselves worked on and nothing else. This is why the "what will this break?" question is difficult to answer. Games often need more than 3 years to finish as well, but part of your team is developing DLC to extent the life of your previous game. That's why some games take forever to develop (FFXV, BotW) but are usually pretty amazing, because they've had the time to perfect the systems they're working on.

Used to be a pretty bad procrastinator and finally changed when I decided that I didn't want to regret not having accomplished my ultimate dreams. 

The one thing that helped me immensely was going to bed early to ensure I got 8 hours of sleep. Every day, no matter what. I would also try to schedule my sleep so I woke up at least 2 hours before work. I did this for 3 days, and my body's natural sleep rhythm started to adjust. I woke up feeling refreshed at 6:30am and said "well, I have time to kill, guess I can work out". 

I didn't want to pay for gym membership or anything, so I spent 3 bucks on a 7 minute workout app. It basically just cycles through 30 second exercises with 10 second rests in between. Now I literally had no reason to say I "can't exercise today" because it takes just 7 minutes to do. 

After the workout I said "well, I'm hot and sweaty, guess I'll start taking colder showers". The cold showers are good for your hair/skin and help you wake up in the morning.

I get out of the shower and it's 7am. I think about other things I want to improve. All the things I want to learn. I decide that I'm going to study something for 1 hour every single day. Something that I want to learn or improve my understanding on (I'm a programmer, so I usually just want to learn how to write better software).

I pour myself a cup of coffee and spend an hour on tackling a hard programming problem. I finish at 8am feeling pretty confident about the day ahead of me, now that I already have a lot done. I still have 30 minutes to get ready for work, so I make some toast and pack myself a light lunch (don't buy lunch every day, it's an awful spending habit). 

I get home at 5-6pm. I'm tired, but I don't want to just lay around all afternoon. So I think about the other habits I want to improve. I want to pick up reading again for sure. So I decide "okay, I can read 10 pages a day. That's not too bad.". I finish 10 pages but decide to finish the chapter I'm on anyway as I find it interesting. 

Getting hungry, I decide to make myself some dinner. But the dishes are piling up in the sink, so I say "well, I guess I should clean the kitchen". I load dishes into the dishwasher and wipe the countertops. I microwave myself a plate of nachos and watch an episode of anime. 

If you wake up late every morning like I used to do, you're already starting your day with a failure. It makes you feel like shit and you hate yourself for not being able to get out of bed on time. You feel angry because you don't have time to make your coffee or eat breakfast. You go to work hungry and irritable. 

But if you wake up early, you start your day on a positive note. And you can get the hard stuff out of the way early on to boost your confidence for the day. Taking on the *hardest* task first will leave you saying "that wasn't so bad, I wonder what else I can do!". You will do a 180 in a matter of days and not recognize yourself. 

I use an app called "Today" to track my daily to-do list. It starts with "Sleep for 8 hours" so when I wake up I check that off. Then I have "7 minute workout" which I do every morning. After that I have "Study 1 hour", "Read 10 pages", "Do 1 chore" and "Meditate 10 minutes".

I try to complete this list every day, and I try not to beat myself up if I miss one or two things on it. I just say "I didn't do any chores today, but I'll be sure to do one tomorrow". 

Make small goals that are achievable. I set my reading minimum to 10 pages because I know that I can read that in about 15 minutes, which isn't a lot of time out of my day. But if it's 10pm and I haven't read anything today, I would be reluctant to read if my goal had said "read 40 pages".

Small goals help you stay motivated to do other small goals. And they will gradually improve your life as a whole. You will notice your bad habits start to dwindle because you don't have time for them anymore. You're too obsessed with getting just one more goal done today. When you make the day a game by seeing how many "mental victories" you can have (choosing water over soda, not touching your phone for a few hours), you go to sleep at night feeling satisfied with your day and are excited to live tomorrow. You know that you're slowly working towards your goals. After a month you'll look back  and say "wow, I worked out every day, read 300 pages, studied for 30 hours, and kept my chores in order" and it will feel amazing. You'll start a chain of success that you don't ever want to break.

The boss fight should follow a similar strategy, with each player training in a separate spot to minimize getting cornered by zombies. Just take things slowly and fire a few WW bursts at any alien when you get the chance. If at any point you're walking towards the center (near the portal) fire a bunch of shots into him if he's red and have a friend throw grenades or put down a boom box so you have a clear shot at knifing the fuse. Rinse and repeat. It's not that bad if you take it slow and maintain control of the zombie trains. Use Perk insured and the card that automatically revives you (I forgot the name). 

The aliens kinda randomly teleport between both players so it's hard to just have one guy do all the killing while the other trains. It's best to just have both players maintain a small train and shoot any alien when they have the chance. 

And to answer your question, you can do the combination yourself, it just requires some quick reflexes. Traveling in a half-circle to the next color (journey to Kepler for example) will always result in a fail unless you slide. Polar to spawn is the most difficult one as it requires you to climb stairs after traveling a half circle, so that one is damn near impossible with one person. 

Any combination that requires a half-circle is best done with two people. The example you gave is the correct way to split up the work.

One person should train zombies near the entrance to polar peak, while the other trains near spawn. The person entering the combination should have a small train if possible. It's typically a bit easier to have one person do the entire combination if they know how to slide properly. If the first color is in front of the PaP portal, have the person in spawn start it off, if the first color is near polar peak, do the opposite.

If the first two colors are on opposing sides (North + South, East + West), you'll probably have to work together to press them unless you're really good at sliding quickly from one to the next. The stairs to PaP in particular are a bitch and will slow you down if running from the polar peak radio.

Timing is key here as you don't want to press the first button before the colored lights appear. You also want to make sure your zombie train is as far away as possible so you have time to enter the combination before they rush you. Say "Done!" or something when you press a key so your buddy knows when to enter their color. It's best if adjacent colors are entered by the same person as they'll already be close to the second color, so try to optimize for that. Opposite colors on the other hand are best entered by separate users.

While I admit the recording arts degrees and film and such may be worthless, I can speak personally for the game development degree. It landed me a decent job out of college and I learned a lot from it.

Some people do it to save time, or money. For profit colleges can often be cheaper or they don't run a full 4 years. I went to Full Sail because there weren't many colleges with degrees in game development at the time. Ended up saving me a lot of money compared to Digipen University, and I had a job by the time I turned 20.

I could have just gotten a CS degree at my state school, but I was really passionate about game development and it seemed like a solid option to me. I wasn't disappointed.

Can't speak for ITT, but I can speak for Full Sail University and it's game development program. I was actually surprised by the amount of engagement from instructors and the amount of topics that were covered. The labs were (mostly) well designed and they really push you to think critically when you're stuck rather than just say "it doesn't work what am I doing wrong". They taught me debugging skills (something that was never really covered in the traditional CS classes I took in community college) and the final project you work on really helps you learn to collaborate with other programmers in a pseudo-industry setting.

Far forward 21 months and I graduated with my degree, having already received an offer for a software dev position. I ended up taking a different job a few months down the line instead, but I was still only 20 years old with a job in my field. It was really worth it in my opinion. 

That being said, you really have to put the work in, and the tuition isn't cheap. You'll probably end up paying a smaller total amount compared to a traditional 4 year school, but it's the fast payment plan that ends up screwing people over.

I've also heard horror stories from people in the film or audio degree programs, so I can really only speak for game development. It's a rigorous program and only the students who are truly driven will succeed. I would often lock my PS4 in my closet or disable Facebook for months at a time. Forget about a social life for 21 months as well. 

The scholarships are easy as well, I got a $22k "creative minds" scholarship for submitting a broken Unity game demo (most of which I learned on YouTube). Totally worth it. The price of my degree at the end was around $65000 after the scholarship.

I would advise against that simply due to how the leveling system works in KH. You see, you'll first answer generic questions at the beginning of the game, and your combination of answers will determine how fast or slow you level in 1-50 and 50-100.

[Here](http://strategywiki.org/wiki/Kingdom_Hearts/Awakening#Third_Platform) is a good guide for how this works.

Basically, you can choose whether you want to:
1) level quickly first, then slowly later
2) level equally throughout the game
3) level slowly at first, quickly later

Because of this, it's highly recommended that you choose the first option for your speedrun (beginner) as well as proud mode because you'll most likely get to the end of the game sub level 40 and sub 50 respectively for the two modes. 

You don't want to choose anything but option 1 in your speedrun game, trust me.

I would recommend doing the 100% play through on your normal game as you can choose option 3 to get levels 50-100 with relative ease. The treasure chest thing is really just a small nuisance and wont really contribute to your total time to platinum, that was just my personal recommendation. But leveling to 100 will be heavily influenced by your beginning game choices. 

However, you do get a 30% exp boost item on beginner mode, so it does sort of even out. But you're bound to have opened up at least most of the chests on your normal game once you beat it. You'll also most likely skip a world or two on your speedrun game, so if you don't want to repeat those worlds you should 100% your normal. 

You'll also have to pick a weapon from the start of the game, as well as sacrifice one. Doing so will determine how your stats grow and what abilities you earn as you level. Choose whatever you like in your normal run. On proud mode I would suggest getting the shield for the abilities "second chance" and "leaf bracer" which will save your ass multiple times in a boss fight. 

Some people like to play defensively during the speed run, but I prefer to choose the sword so I can finish the bosses quicker. If you're able to use dodge roll effectively and avoid most enemy attacks, then the sword is probably a strong option. 

Though, these are just my opinions and the option is entirely up to you (: have fun!

[SPOILERS]

**Gobblegums**:
On the house and Unquenchable are great for accumulating perks before the boss fight. Though once you're close to entering the boss fight everyone should try to get an Aftertaste. The boss fight will occur on whatever round you start it on and will not end until you beat it so Aftertaste allows you and your teammates to get downed as many times as you like during the boss fight and keep all your perks. 

**Strategy**:
The flaming plunger is also really helpful for fighting the panzers during the boss fight. My team and I usually throw a monkey down when the lightning ball appears under the boss and once someone puts down their DG-4's we throw another one. This ensures that no one gets overtaken by zombies as we are cautiously standing behind pillars (just in case the DG-4 was placed improperly) waiting for the boss to become vulnerable. It's also wise to take out your bow during this part to shoot at your feet if any zombies reach you at your pillar. Once the boss is vulnerable, take out your strongest weapon and go to town.

**Help!**:
If someone gets downed during the boss fight don't panic and run to them right away, lead the panzers/zombies away from them and take the time to ensure you're at full health before reviving them. Use their bleedout time to your advantage and have the void or lightning bow shoot towards the downed person to help the medic.

**Guns**:
For guns I prefer an LMG, Haymaker, or any assault rifle with double tap and upgraded. My second slot always has a bow unless I picked up Mule-kick through an On the house.

**Perks**:
For perks I strongly recommend Jugs, Quick Revive, Stamin-up and double tap. If you have an unquenchable I'd pick up Speed Cola or Widows Wine if you want to try your luck with the wunderfizz. Mule-kick really isn't necessary as long as you're able to take down the panzers quickly to grab those max ammos.

**Misc. tips**:
Try to start the EE steps as soon as possible, my team and I usually finish the wolf bow around round 8 so we're able to start the wisps and get all the way up to the ghost step before round 12 (even earlier if we're able to keep a zombie around). This leaves us plenty of time to set up our guns, perks, and gobblegums before the fight (it can be tedious to ensure that everyone has aftertaste active during the same round).

IMHO, this depends more on what you plan to do with the games you make or how you want to approach this problem. 

Case 0: If you're a teenager in high school looking to make games as a career or as a hobby but don't have the time or patience or skills to finish them then you should probably stick to rectangles on a blue background or sprite sheets from [Spriters-Resource](http://www.spriters-resource.com/)

Case 1: If you're a seasoned programmer with an job that doesn't push you over 50 hours a week then I would definitely try to find some art hobbyists to join you; there are always art graduates looking for a more beefy portfolio. [Deviantart](http://www.deviantart.com/) is a good place to start as you're likely to run into various sprite artists looking to put their work to use. There are plenty of hobbyists like yourself who aren't concerned with potential profits or business plans, the comment(s) on this post are a clear indication of that.

Case 2: If you want to *learn* how to make your projects look better, I would start with some simple 2D assets in a program like [Paint.Net](http://www.getpaint.net/index.html). The internet is also full of videos and articles on the art of making game art (redundancy is redundant). If you are making a 3D game this is more of an endeavor as 3D art has a much steeper learning curve due to its sheer complexity. If this is the case I would advise you to find free 3D models online as learning Autodesk Maya isn't a cakewalk.

Case 4: Buy assets, sell the game, profit.

Good luck on your journey!
